title: Let the Index Serve the ORDER BY
description: An INCLUDE column can cover a query but only a KEY column provides order; key the index on the ORDER BY column to remove the Sort. Why it matters: "filter then sort" is an everyday query shape, and this is a common, easy-to-miss reason a seemingly well-indexed query still pays for an expensive sort.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About

This lesson is about a subtle distinction that catches a lot of people off guard: an index can genuinely make your query *faster* (help it seek instead of scan) while still leaving behind an expensive `Sort` operation in the plan — because filtering rows and ordering rows are two different jobs, and an index only helps with ordering if it's built the right way for that specific purpose.

The scenario: `SELECT OrderId, OrderDate, Total FROM Orders WHERE CustomerId = 100 ORDER BY OrderDate DESC`, with an index `IX_Orders_CustomerId (CustomerId) INCLUDE (OrderDate, Total)`. This index does everything you'd think it should — it lets the query seek straight to customer 100's rows (because `CustomerId` is the key/searchable column), and it even *covers* the query (because `OrderDate` and `Total` are tagged along via `INCLUDE`, so no Key Lookup is needed — see the covering-index lesson for that concept). And yet, the plan still shows a separate `Sort` step to put the results in `OrderDate DESC` order. Why, if the index already has everything?

The key idea is that there are two very different roles a column can play in an index: it can be a **key column** (part of the actual sorted structure of the index — think of this as "the columns the index is physically sorted by"), or it can be an **included column** (extra data carried along for convenience, not part of the sort order at all — like a sticky note attached to each index entry, present for reference but not affecting where that entry sits in the structure). In this lesson's index, `CustomerId` is a key column (the index is sorted by it), but `OrderDate` and `Total` are only *included*, not key columns — meaning the index has no guarantee at all about what order `OrderDate` values appear in among rows that share the same `CustomerId`. They're just tagging along, unordered, however they happened to land physically.

So when your query asks for the rows ordered by `OrderDate DESC`, the index gives SQL Server the *right rows* efficiently (that part is solved by the seek), but it gives no guarantee whatsoever about what *order* those rows come out in with respect to `OrderDate`, because `OrderDate` was never part of the sort key. SQL Server still has to take whatever set of rows it found and explicitly sort them by `OrderDate` afterward, which is a real, separate operation — a `Sort` — that costs CPU and, for large row sets, potentially memory or even tempdb (a special system database SQL Server uses as scratch space when a sort or other operation doesn't fit in the memory it was given — sorts that spill to tempdb are noticeably slower because now you're reading and writing to disk-backed storage instead of doing everything in memory).

The fix is to make `OrderDate` part of the index's actual *key*, not just an included column: build the index as `(CustomerId, OrderDate) INCLUDE (Total)` instead. Now the index is sorted first by customer, and *within* each customer, sorted by date — exactly the two things this query cares about, in exactly the right combination. SQL Server can seek to customer 100's block of rows, and because that block is already internally sorted by `OrderDate`, it can simply walk through it in the needed direction (there's a neat trick here: an index sorted ascending can still satisfy a `DESC` request efficiently, because SQL Server can just walk the B-tree structure backwards — reading a sorted structure in reverse is still cheap, it doesn't require re-sorting). No separate `Sort` operator is needed at all — the rows come out of the index already in the right order.

This connects to the same underlying principle as composite key ordering more generally: what you put in the *key* portion of an index (versus the `INCLUDE` portion) isn't just about "does the index contain this data" — it's about "does the physical order of the index match what my query needs." A column can be present in an index and still be useless for sorting if it's only carried along as an included column rather than woven into the sort key itself.

Why does this matter in real applications? "Filter by one thing, then sort by another" (customer's orders, newest first; a user's messages, most recent first; a product's reviews, highest rated first) is one of the single most common query shapes in any application with lists, feeds, or dashboards. Recognizing "there's a Sort operator in my plan even though I have an index" as a sign that your key column order doesn't match your `ORDER BY` is a very high-value pattern to know.

A simple way to build intuition here is to think about a library's card catalog sorted by author's last name. If you ask "give me all books by Tolkien, sorted by publication year," a catalog sorted purely by author name gets you straight to the Tolkien section — but within that section, the cards might be in whatever order they were originally filed, not sorted by year at all. You'd still have to pull all the Tolkien cards out and manually sort them afterward. But if the catalog had been organized "by author, and then by year within each author," you'd get exactly what you asked for with no extra sorting step. That's the entire difference between a key column and an included column in an index: key columns define the actual physical ordering you can rely on; included columns are just extra facts tagged along for convenience. Whenever your query both filters by one thing and sorts by another, it's worth explicitly asking whether your index's key column order reflects *both* of those needs, in the right sequence — not just whether the sort column happens to be present somewhere in the index at all.

One more thing worth internalizing: the cost of a Sort operator isn't fixed -- it grows with the number of rows being sorted and can be made worse if SQL Server underestimates how much memory the sort needs, forcing it to spill intermediate results out to tempdb (disk-backed scratch space) rather than keeping everything in fast memory. So eliminating an unnecessary Sort by fixing your index's key order isn't just about raw operator count -- it can also protect you from a much worse, memory-pressure-driven slowdown under real production load.

## Scenario
`SELECT OrderId, OrderDate, Total FROM Orders WHERE CustomerId = 100 ORDER BY OrderDate DESC` seeks one customer's orders and sorts them newest-first. The index `IX_Orders_CustomerId (CustomerId) INCLUDE (OrderDate, Total)` even *covers* the query — yet the plan still contains a **Sort**.

## Why it's slow
The index is keyed only on `CustomerId`. `OrderDate` and `Total` are **INCLUDE** columns: they ride along in the leaf level so the query is covered, but they impose **no order**. So the seek returns customer 100's rows in whatever physical order they sit — and SQL Server must add a **Sort** to satisfy `ORDER BY OrderDate`. At 100 rows the Sort is cheap, but the same pattern over thousands of rows per key needs a memory grant and can spill to tempdb.

## What to look for
- A **Sort** operator sitting on top of an Index Seek, ordering by a column the index doesn't key on.
- The ORDER BY column present only as an INCLUDE, not in the index key.

## The concept
Make the sort column part of the **key**, right after the equality column: `(CustomerId, OrderDate)`. Now the seek on `CustomerId = 100` returns rows already ordered by `OrderDate`, and `ORDER BY OrderDate DESC` becomes a free backward scan of that range — the **Sort disappears**. The rule: an INCLUDE column can *cover* a query, but only a **key** column can provide *order*.
startingQuery: SELECT OrderId, OrderDate, Total FROM Orders WHERE CustomerId = 100 ORDER BY OrderDate DESC;
hints: The index covers the query, but OrderDate is only an INCLUDE column -- included columns carry data, not order.
Because the seeked rows aren't ordered by OrderDate, the plan adds a Sort to satisfy ORDER BY.
Rebuild the index as (CustomerId, OrderDate) so OrderDate is a key column and the ORDER BY needs no Sort.
